newsitem.title: UK: Nothing new in Africa for British troops.
newsitem.headline: Nothing new in Africa for British troops.

text.p: The British army's involvement in a planned humanitarian mission to Zaire is its latest venture into a continent that has often dealt harshly with military intervention from Britain.
A small reconnaissance party set off on Friday to see what part British troops might play in an international effort to feed more than a million starving people in central Africa.
They went with the words of Conservative member of parliament Ian Duncan Smith, who served in the Commonwealth monitoring force in Zimbabwe in 1979-80, ringing in their ears.
"When the troops get to that continent, what they find on the ground is something considerably more difficult than has possibly been imagined by those sitting in Whitehall," he said in parliament.
Even though Britain wielded power across the length and breadth of Africa for many years, the continent never lost its ability to make life difficult for its colonial masters.
A glance in the history books, or even a conversation with some of the British soldiers who went to help rebuild Rwanda two years ago, will have told troops what to expect.
"What went on here is ghastly. It defies belief. You can hardly believe it happened unless you saw it," was how Major Mark Hiskett summed up his time in a country racked by a genocidal bloodbath.
Reminiscences of British soldiers confronted by the horrors of Kenya's pre-independence Mau-Mau revolt in the early 1950s are couched in similar terms.
Sergeant Harry Whitehead recalled how he and his men found the bodies of two African soldiers murdered by the insurgents when they stopped in a bar for a drink.

"Congealed blood lay everywhere, on the floor, splashed on the walls... It was like an abattoir and stank to high heaven. We found the bodies, bloated and mutilated, in a nearby ditch," he said in memoirs quoted by historian Robin Neillands.

Ever since red-coated British soldiers defied Zulu warriors at Rorke's Drift in 1879, Africa has evoked a powerful fascination, sharpened by a good deal of ignorance, in the British popular imagination.
"Does more than one person in a hundred have the faintest idea what is going on in central Africa," asked columnist Stephen Glover in the Daily Telegrpah.
A report from Zaire in Friday's Times said British troops could expect to be confronted by members of the exotic Mai Tai tribe.
"These tribesmen, in monkey skins and coated with white paint, wave their penises at their enemies and think they are bullet-proof," the paper's correspondent warned.
But fanatical tribemen are nothing new to British soldiers venturing into the African interior.
More than a century ago, troops under Major-General Charles "Chinese" Gordon in Sudan faced hordes of Mahdists untroubled by the fatal consequences of charging British guns in a full frontal assault.
News that cholera has broken out in the hospital wards of Goma in eastern Zaire also finds an echo in the history of the British army's involvement in Africa.

Viscount Wolseley defeated the Ashanti in 1874, but victory had to be achieved in a hurry before his troops fell victim to the ever-present spectre of fever in the mangrove swamps along the West African coast.
